summary: For 10–11 year-olds, teach reading of geological diagrams (not fact memorisation): label Earth's interior cross-section (crust, mantle, outer core, inner core); apply superposition to sedimentary strata (deepest = oldest, top = youngest); and trace pathways on a rock-cycle diagram. The load-bearing insight is that an undisturbed strata cross-section is a slice through time — reading up the layers reads forward through Earth's history. A route recommended by the source pedagogy is to have children build strata themselves (deposit sediment episode by episode over 'millions of years', embed fossils), then read the finished stack as a record of events in order; this is a proposed approach rather than a format proven superior to others. Keep the two diagram types distinct: Earth's interior is a spatial cross-section, while strata are a time record.
misconceptions: 'The top layer is oldest' — reversing superposition.
Confusing Earth's interior layers (crust/mantle/core) with sedimentary strata — two different kinds of 'layers'.
'A cross-section shows what's on the surface' — not reading it as a cut-through view.
'Rock layers formed all at once' — missing that each stratum records a separate episode over long time.
'The rock cycle has a fixed one-way order' — not seeing it as a network of reversible pathways.
'Deeper always means the mantle/core' — conflating shallow sedimentary depth with planetary-scale depth.

activities.title: Build strata over time, then read the finished column
steps: Deposit layers in sequence across 'millions of years': lay a sandy beach layer, then a layer of volcanic ash, then a muddy seabed on top, giving each layer an era label.
Drop an early marker fossil (e.g. a trilobite) into one of the first layers and a clearly later fossil (e.g. a dinosaur bone) into a layer added later.
Stop depositing and switch to reading the finished cross-section: point to the layer that was laid down first and the one laid down last.
State and justify the rule: the deepest layer is oldest and the top is youngest, because each new layer settled on top of the ones already there.
Predict: if a river dumped new mud here next year, where would the new layer form, and would it be the oldest or youngest?
activities.insight: An undisturbed strata cross-section is a record of events in order: because you watched the bottom layer arrive first, deepest = oldest and reading up the cliff reads forward through time. In this undisturbed stack, the deeper a fossil lies, the older it is.

activities.title: Read then draw: separate labelling from reading the order
steps: Given a cross-section of four stacked rock layers, point to the layer laid down first and say which clue in the diagram shows it.
Explain in words how lower layers must have formed before the ones above them.
Draw where the next new layer to form would go.
Then consider a diagram where the layers are bent and tilted: decide whether the layer that was originally lowest is still the oldest, and explain your reasoning.
activities.insight: Reading the age order and knowing where new material is added are separate skills; a learner may label layers yet still read the stack top-down. New sediment is added on top, not underneath. Deformation (bending/tilting) after deposition does not change which layer was originally lowest and therefore oldest, though it can mean current depth on the page no longer matches age, so reason from the original deposition order.

activities.title: Label Earth's interior and keep it separate from strata
steps: On a cross-section of Earth's interior, label crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core, and state one property of each.
Explicitly compare the two diagram types: Earth's interior is a spatial cross-section of the whole planet; sedimentary strata are a time record of deposited layers.
Decide whether 'deeper = older' applies to the crust–mantle–core diagram, and explain why superposition applies to deposited strata but not to Earth's internal structure.
activities.insight: Earth's interior layers (crust/mantle/core) and sedimentary strata are two different kinds of 'layers'. Superposition's deeper=older rule is about deposited sediment, not about the planet's internal structure, so it should not be applied to the core.

activities.title: Trace rock-cycle pathways as a network
steps: On a rock-cycle diagram, trace a route for a rock moving between igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic states.
Name the process that drives each transition you cross (e.g. heat and pressure, melting then cooling, weathering and erosion then deposition, compaction and cementation).
Find more than one possible pathway between two rock types to show the cycle is a network, not a single fixed one-way order.
activities.insight: Rock types can be transformed through multiple possible pathways, often through intervening stages, driven by named processes. The cycle is a network rather than one fixed sequence; this does not mean each process simply runs backward.

checkQuestion: Here is a cross-section showing four stacked rock layers. Point to the layer that was laid down first and tell me how the diagram shows it — then draw where the next new layer to form would go.
checkAnswer: Points to the bottom layer as the oldest / first deposited, explaining that lower layers were laid down before the ones above them (superposition); then draws the next new layer on top of the stack.
